Compromised jscrambler 8.14.0 npm Release Drops Rust Infostealer During Install

The Hacker News
2026-07-11 13 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Version&nbsp;8.14.0&nbsp;of the jscrambler npm package shipped with a malicious&nbsp;preinstall&nbsp;hook that silently drops and runs a native infostealer during installation, one build each for Windows, macOS, and Linux. Published on July 11, 2026, it needs no import and no CLI call. Installing 8.14.0 is enough to run&nbsp;it. Socket flagged the release&nbsp;six minutes after it was

npm preinstall hook (dist/setup.js) drops & launches native binary from temp AIInstallation High
Hunts the jscrambler@8.14.0 supply-chain execution chain: a Node/npm process running the malicious dist/setup.js loader spawning an unsigned child binary out of the system temp directory. This is the article-specific install-time behaviour that fires the moment the poisoned package is installed on any client that still runs install scripts. Rationale: Anchors on the two article-named strings that no benign install produces together: the parent command line referencing dist/setup.js and a child binary executing from temp. Loader mechanism corroborated by StepSecurity/SafeDep/Socket writeups (package diff shows dist/setup.js + dist/intro.js). Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/incidents • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/malicious-npm-packages-fetch-infostealer-for-windows-linux-macos/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1204.003 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate npm packages with benign postinstall/preinstall build steps that shell out to a temp scratch dir (e.g. node-gyp native compiles writing to %TEMP%)
  • node-based test runners that spawn helper binaries from an OS temp path during CI
  • Electron/pkg self-extracting apps unpacking to temp on first run
  • In-house build tooling whose loader is coincidentally named setup.js
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "node-gyp" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "prebuild-install")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent command line references dist/setup.js and the child is an unsigned binary with a random/hidden name under temp; pull the package-manager log on the host and grep for jscrambler@8.14.0 install events on/after 2026-07-11. 2) Contain: isolate the host/CI runner, kill the temp process and its scheduled task, and treat every secret reachable by the build (cloud keys, npm/GitHub tokens, AI-tool/MCP keys) as stolen — begin rotation. 3) Hunt: sweep other build hosts for jscrambler@8.14.0 in lockfiles/caches and pivot on the child binary's SHA256 and the two C2 IPs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("dist\\setup.js","dist/setup.js")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", "/tmp/", "/var/folders/", "/private/tmp/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has "node"
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("dist\\setup.js","dist/setup.js")
| where ActingProcessName has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", "/tmp/", "/var/folders/", "/private/tmp/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Known jscrambler infostealer payload/loader hashes on disk or in execution AIInstallation Medium
High-fidelity IOC sweep for the five published SHA-256 hashes tied to jscrambler@8.14.0: the setup.js loader, the intro.js binary container, and the decompressed Linux/Windows/macOS Rust stealer payloads. Matches on either file write or process execution so it catches the artifact whether it merely landed or actually ran. Rationale: Uses the five exact SHA-256 IOCs published for jscrambler@8.14.0 (setup.js, intro.js, and the three decompressed OS payloads); hash equality is essentially zero-FP. Loader/payload structure corroborated by StepSecurity/Socket. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/incidents
ATT&CKT1204.003 T1027.013
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • None expected under normal conditions — exact SHA-256 collisions do not occur benignly
  • Security-team detonation/sandbox VM intentionally executing the sample (whitelist known analysis hosts)
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling that stores the sample file on a research host
  • Backup/AV quarantine copies re-scanned and re-hashed
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("MALWARE-LAB-01","SANDBOX-DETONATION")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the matched hash and whether Source=ProcessExec (payload ran) vs FileWrite (only landed); check for the jscrambler@8.14.0 install event that preceded it. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate/quarantine the matched artifact and any child process, and remove the persistence (scheduled task / LaunchAgent). 3) Hunt: pivot on the same hash across the fleet, then pull outbound connections from that process to identify C2 (37.27.122.124 / 57.128.246.79) and scope secret exposure.

Outbound C2 to jscrambler stealer hard-coded IPs (37.27.122.124 / 57.128.246.79) AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any host — especially build/CI runners — connecting outbound to the two hard-coded attacker IPs StepSecurity observed the dropped Rust stealer beacon to over TLS. Direct network IOC match tied to this campaign's exfiltration channel. Rationale: Two hard-coded destination IPs are the only published network IOCs for the campaign (StepSecurity runtime monitoring). Marked Medium confidence / Medium in the C2 field because the IPs are effectively single-sourced to StepSecurity; keep but review before hard-blocking to avoid hosting-provider overlap. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/incidents
ATT&CKT1571 T1041 T1573.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Shared-hosting/VPS provider IP reuse where a benign service later occupies the same address (Hetzner/OVH ranges)
  • Security scanners or threat-intel validation tooling deliberately probing the IOC IPs
  • A researcher pulling the sample and detonating on a monitored host
  • Proxy/egress appliance health-checks against blocklisted IPs
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — if it is an unsigned temp-dir binary parented by node/setup.js, treat as confirmed stealer beacon; note egress byte volume for exfil sizing. 2) Contain: block both IPs at the egress firewall/proxy, isolate the host/runner, and kill the process plus its persistence. 3) Hunt: search DNS for check.torproject.org / archive.torproject.org from the same host, scope other hosts touching these IPs, and rotate all secrets the CI/build context could reach.

jscrambler stealer persistence: hidden every-minute scheduled task / macOS LaunchAgent from temp AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the two persistence mechanisms the stealer installs: a hidden Windows scheduled task set to relaunch every minute pointing at the temp-dir payload, and a macOS LaunchAgent plist written into ~/Library/LaunchAgents by a process running from a temp path. Article-specific by combining the every-minute cadence and temp-directory target. Rationale: Combines the article's specific persistence traits — an every-minute Windows task and a macOS LaunchAgent — with the requirement that the target/creator lives in temp, which is what makes it stealer-specific rather than generic task creation. Persistence mechanism corroborated by StepSecurity/SafeDep. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/incidents
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1543.001 T1564.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit software creating high-frequency maintenance tasks (rare at 1-minute cadence, but some monitoring agents do)
  • Developers testing scheduled-task creation from a temp build output during CI
  • macOS app installers legitimately dropping a LaunchAgent, if run from a temp-extracted installer
  • Endpoint management tools staging helper binaries in temp then registering persistence
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\node_modules\\.bin" and Detail !has "MicrosoftEdgeUpdate"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the task action / LaunchAgent ProgramArguments — confirm it points at a hidden random-named binary in temp; on Windows check Task Scheduler for the hidden flag. 2) Contain: delete the scheduled task / LaunchAgent plist, kill the referenced binary, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: pivot on the referenced binary's SHA256 and its outbound connections (C2 IPs / Tor), and check other hosts for the same task name or LaunchAgent label.

( DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
  | where ProcessCommandLine has "/create"
  | where ProcessCommandLine has "minute"
  | where ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Kind="WinSchedTask", Detail=ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath ),
( DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ActionType == "FileCreated"
  | where FolderPath has "/Library/LaunchAgents/"
  | where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/tmp/", "/var/folders/", "/private/tmp/")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Kind="macLaunchAgent", Detail=FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFolderPath )
| order by Timestamp desc
union
( ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where ActingProcessName has "schtasks.exe"
  | where ActingProcessCommandLine has "/create" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "minute"
  | where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\")
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, Kind="WinSchedTask", Detail=ActingProcessCommandLine ),
( ImFileEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where TargetFilePath has "/Library/LaunchAgents/"
  | where ActingProcessName has_any ("/tmp/", "/var/folders/", "/private/tmp/")
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername=ActingProcessName, Kind="macLaunchAgent", Detail=TargetFilePath )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" Processes.process="*/create*" (Processes.process="*minute*") (Processes.process="*\\Temp\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" Processes.process="*/create*" (Processes.process="*minute*") (Processes.process="*\\Temp\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Temp-dir binary harvesting AI-tool/MCP configs and cloud/wallet secrets AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the stealer's credential-collection stage: a single short-lived process running from the system temp directory reading across disparate secret stores in one burst — AI coding-tool configs (Claude Desktop, Cursor, Windsurf, VS Code, Zed) holding API keys and MCP credentials, cloud CLI config (.aws/.azure/gcloud), Bitwarden, browser credential DBs, and crypto wallets (MetaMask/Phantom/Exodus). The AI-tool/MCP config sweep is the novel, campaign-specific behaviour. Rationale: Targets the article's stand-out behaviour — one temp-dir process fanning out across AI-tool/MCP config files plus cloud CLI creds, Bitwarden, browser DBs and crypto wallets. The AI-tool config angle (Claude/Cursor/Windsurf/Zed) is explicitly called out as novel in the article and by StepSecurity/SafeDep; the >=3-distinct-store threshold suppresses single benign reads. Sigma omitted (threshold + aggregation shape). Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/incidents
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1552.001 T1528 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit dev tooling or backup agents scanning home-dir configs (dotfile sync, secret scanners like gitleaks) if run from a temp path
  • An IDE or AI assistant itself reading its own config plus .aws during normal operation (usually not from temp)
  • Endpoint DLP/inventory agents enumerating credential stores
  • Password-manager migration/export utilities touching multiple vault paths
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gitleaks.exe","trufflehog.exe","code.exe","cursor.exe","claude.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reading process is an unsigned random-named binary in temp (not a signed IDE/agent) and review the set of stores touched; correlate with a jscrambler@8.14.0 install on the host. 2) Contain: isolate the host and treat every touched secret as stolen — rotate AWS/Azure/GCP keys, npm/GitHub tokens, AI-tool and MCP API keys; revoke Bitwarden/browser/Discord/Slack sessions; move crypto out of affected wallets. 3) Hunt: pivot on the binary hash and its C2 egress, and sweep the fleet for the same temp-process credential fan-out pattern.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", "/tmp/", "/var/folders/", "/private/tmp/")
| extend SecretStore = case(
    FolderPath has_any ("Claude","Cursor","Windsurf",".vscode","Code\\User","Zed"), "AITool_MCP",
    FolderPath has ".aws", "AWS",
    FolderPath has_any ("gcloud","gcp"), "GCP",
    FolderPath has ".azure", "Azure",
    FolderPath has "Bitwarden", "Bitwarden",
    FolderPath has_any ("MetaMask","Phantom","Exodus"), "Wallet",
    FolderPath has_any ("Login Data","Cookies","key4.db","logins.json"), "Browser",
    "")
| where SecretStore != ""
| summarize StoresTouched=dcount(SecretStore), Stores=make_set(SecretStore,10), SamplePaths=make_set(FolderPath,15), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| where StoresTouched >= 3
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", "/tmp/", "/var/folders/", "/private/tmp/")
| extend SecretStore = case(
    TargetFilePath has_any ("Claude","Cursor","Windsurf",".vscode","Code/User","Zed"), "AITool_MCP",
    TargetFilePath has ".aws", "AWS",
    TargetFilePath has_any ("gcloud","gcp"), "GCP",
    TargetFilePath has ".azure", "Azure",
    TargetFilePath has "Bitwarden", "Bitwarden",
    TargetFilePath has_any ("MetaMask","Phantom","Exodus"), "Wallet",
    TargetFilePath has_any ("Login Data","Cookies","key4.db","logins.json"), "Browser",
    "")
| where SecretStore != ""
| summarize StoresTouched=dcount(SecretStore), Stores=make_set(SecretStore,10), SamplePaths=make_set(TargetFilePath,15), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessId, ActingProcessName
| where StoresTouched >= 3
| order by FirstSeen desc
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo ContextImageFileName=/(\\Temp\\|\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\|\/tmp\/|\/var\/folders\/)/i
| regex("(Claude|Cursor|Windsurf|\\.vscode|Zed|\\.aws|\\.azure|gcloud|Bitwarden|MetaMask|Phantom|Exodus|Login Data|key4\\.db)", field=TargetFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextProcessId, ContextImageFileName], function=count(field=TargetFileName, distinct=true))
| _count >= 3

| tstats summariesonly=false values(Filesystem.file_path) as paths dc(Filesystem.file_path) as distinct_paths min(_time) as firstTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.process_path="*\\Temp\\*" OR Filesystem.process_path="*/tmp/*" OR Filesystem.process_path="*/var/folders/*") (Filesystem.file_path="*\\.aws*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.azure*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*gcloud*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*Claude*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*Cursor*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*Windsurf*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*Zed*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*Bitwarden*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*MetaMask*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*Phantom*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*Exodus*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_id Filesystem.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where distinct_paths >= 3 | convert ctime(firstTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.

DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

ImFileEvent

                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"

      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"

        | where SHA256 in~ ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60", "a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86", "fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or SHA1 in~ ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60", "a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86", "fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or MD5 in~ ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60", "a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86", "fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,

        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60", "a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86", "fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or SHA1 in~ ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60", "a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86", "fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or MD5 in~ ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60", "a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86", "fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60", "a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86", "fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

cms_plugin.exe Rust stager execution + payload pull from 193.42.25.65 AIInstallation High
Hunts the custom 'cms_plugin.exe' implant that masqueraded as a Complaint Management System portal update on Balochistan Police infrastructure. The Rust stager variant downloads a next stage from 193.42.25.65 and prints 'Update Complete! Please refresh the page'. Fires on the named binary executing or any host reaching the stager download IP. Rationale: cms_plugin.exe is a unique implant filename and 193.42.25.65 is the confirmed Rust-stager download server named in the SentinelLABS report; both are non-generic, so a match is effectively a true positive. Cross-checked SentinelOne report and The Record write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/one-target-china-india-espionage-converge-on-pakistani-law-enforcement/ • https://therecord.media/china-india-ran-separate-spy-campaigns-against-same-police-force
ATT&CKT1105 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimately-named plugin binary in an unrelated product also called cms_plugin.exe (rare; validate hash and path)
  • Security researcher / IR analyst detonating the sample in a sandbox VM enrolled in EDR
  • Threat-intel enrichment appliance actively probing 193.42.25.65 for research
  • Proxy/NAT egress IP collision where 193.42.25.65 is re-used by a benign CDN in future (validate at trigger time)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Sandbox\\" and DeviceName !in~ ("IR-SANDBOX-01")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the process tree, SHA256, and folder path for cms_plugin.exe; confirm parent (likely w3wp.exe/web-app service on a CMS/web server) and whether the host is an internet-facing police web application server. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block 193.42.25.65 at the perimeter, and preserve the binary for reversing. 3) Hunt: sweep all web servers for cms_plugin.exe uploads, search web logs on cms.balochistanpolice.gov.pk-style portals for the file, and pivot on the SHA1s and the full campaign C2 IP set (see C2 UC).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "193.42.25.65" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "cms_plugin.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
union
(SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where tolower(NewProcessName) endswith "\\cms_plugin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, Signal="process", NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, Dest=""),
(CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "193.42.25.65"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer=SourceHostName, Account=SourceUserName, Signal="network", NewProcessName=ProcessName, CommandLine="", ParentProcessName="", Dest=DestinationIP)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Fake 360Safe.exe (.NET) reflectively loading AsyncRAT AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the second cms_plugin.exe variant: a .NET executable that masquerades as '360Safe.exe' (a legitimate Qihoo 360 Total Security binary) to reflectively load an in-memory AsyncRAT client. Detects a process named 360Safe.exe whose file metadata is NOT Qihoo/360 or which runs from outside the legitimate 360 install path. Rationale: The report states one implant variant masquerades specifically as 360Safe.exe (Qihoo 360) to reflectively load AsyncRAT; a 360Safe.exe binary running outside the genuine Qihoo install path (or lacking Qihoo file metadata) is a high-fidelity masquerade signal, especially in a Pakistani gov environment unlikely to run Chinese AV. Corroborated by SentinelOne report and Kaspersky's Mysterious Elephant AsyncRAT/Remcos tradecraft. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/one-target-china-india-espionage-converge-on-pakistani-law-enforcement/ • https://securelist.com/mysterious-elephant-apt-ttps-and-tools/117596/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1620
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Qihoo 360 Total Security installed to a non-default drive/path (validate publisher signature)
  • Portable/standalone 360 Total Security run from a USB or Downloads folder by a user
  • Software-deployment tool staging the real 360Safe.exe in a temp cache before install
  • AV bake-off / procurement testing of 360 Total Security by IT
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has_any ("360","Qihoo"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the digital signature and ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName of the 360Safe.exe image — genuine is signed by Qihoo/360; the implant will be unsigned or mis-signed. Inspect for .NET/CLR module loads and outbound connections. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture memory (AsyncRAT is in-memory), block associated C2 IPs. 3) Hunt: search DeviceImageLoadEvents for clr.dll/mscoree loading into 360Safe.exe, and correlate with cms_plugin.exe drops and the campaign C2 IP set.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "360Safe.exe"
| where not(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has_any ("360","Qihoo")) or FolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, ProcessVersionInfoProductName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where tolower(NewProcessName) endswith "\\360safe.exe"
| where not(tolower(NewProcessName) startswith "c:\\program files (x86)\\360\\") and not(tolower(NewProcessName) startswith "c:\\program files\\360\\")
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

Beaconing to Balochistan Police espionage C2 / stager IP set AICommand & Control High
Hunts outbound connections to the confirmed command-and-control and staging IPs across the four converging clusters (Cobalt Strike C2 142.171.183.8, Rust-stager host 193.42.25.65, plus the campaign infrastructure block) targeting Pakistani law enforcement. Any internal host reaching these IPs warrants investigation. Rationale: 142.171.183.8 is the named Cobalt Strike C2 and 193.42.25.65 the stager host; the remaining IPs are the pre-extracted campaign infrastructure. These are static, second-source-consistent IOCs, so egress to any of them is high-fidelity for this specific converging-actor campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/one-target-china-india-espionage-converge-on-pakistani-law-enforcement/ • https://therecord.media/china-india-ran-separate-spy-campaigns-against-same-police-force
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An IOC IP later reassigned to a shared hosting/CDN provider serving benign sites (re-validate WHOIS at trigger time)
  • Internal threat-intel platform or vulnerability scanner actively probing the C2 IPs
  • Security researcher pivoting on the infrastructure from a corporate egress IP
  • Firewall/proxy that logs a blocked (denied) attempt — confirm DeviceAction/outcome is allow before escalating
Suppression filter
DeviceNetworkEvents | where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt") and RemoteIPType == "Public"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source host and the InitiatingProcess making the connection; check whether the connection succeeded vs was blocked, and beacon regularity (jitter/interval). 2) Contain: block all listed IPs at the perimeter, isolate any host with a successful/repeated connection, and snapshot memory for the process (PlugX/ShadowPad/Cobalt Strike/AsyncRAT are memory-resident). 3) Hunt: pivot on the initiating process hash against the campaign SHA1 list, sweep for cms_plugin.exe and fake 360Safe.exe, and review the FortiMail email gateway and web-app servers for the initial foothold.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("142.171.183.8","193.42.25.65","41.216.188.140","89.31.121.220","45.125.32.218","172.111.233.36","172.111.233.96","172.111.233.12","172.111.233.105","172.111.233.26","172.94.9.49","172.94.9.43","172.94.9.19","45.74.6.17")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Conns=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort,10) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by LastSeen desc

| order by LastSeen desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

Critical

jscrambler npm package publishes malicious preinstall binary

StepSecurity
2026-07-11 13 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

On July 11, 2026, version 8.14.0 of jscrambler was published to npm carrying a malicious preinstall hook that drops and executes a platform-specific native binary on Linux, Windows, and macOS. jscrambler is the official CLI client for the Jscrambler Code Integrity API, a commercial JavaScript obfuscation and web-app protection service, with a clean version history dating back to 0.1.0. The compromised release was flagged by StepSecurity's AI Release Analyzer with a suspicion score of 0 (the maximum suspicion rating) on publish.

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Malicious jscrambler@8.14.0 native payload container (dist/intro.js) dropped on install
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — jscrambler npm package publishes malicious preinstall binary
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Detached temp-dir dotfile stealer launched by npm/node preinstall hook · Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] jscrambler stealer C2 egress to hardcoded IPs and Tor endpoints · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Temp-dir stealer reading Chrome/Firefox credential stores and MetaMask wallet vault · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process
Malicious jscrambler@8.14.0 native payload container (dist/intro.js) dropped on install AIDelivery Medium
Hunts installation of the trojanized jscrambler npm package by surfacing creation of the 7.8 MB fake dist/intro.js binary container inside node_modules/jscrambler and the three extracted platform payload hashes. Article-specific because it anchors on the exact package path and the SHA256s of the Rust stealer smuggled behind a .js extension. Rationale: Anchors on the exact malicious artifact node_modules/jscrambler/dist/intro.js and the three extracted payload SHA256s from the IOC table — file path is unique to this package structure and cannot occur legitimately (jscrambler ships no such binary). Hashes lacked an independent second source, so they're OR'd with the article-specific path rather than shipped alone. Cross-checked against: • https://www.npmjs.com/package/jscrambler • https://socket.dev/npm/package/jscrambler/alerts/6.4.28
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1036.008
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher intentionally detonating the sample in a sandbox (expected in malware-analysis VMs)
  • EDR/AV quarantine copies of the extracted payload retaining the original SHA256 in a quarantine folder
  • Backup/restore of an infected node_modules tree replaying the intro.js file-create event
  • A file-integrity tool re-hashing an already-collected sample in a forensics share
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Windows Defender\" and FolderPath !has "quarantine"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm jscrambler is pinned to 8.14.0 in package-lock.json and that dist/intro.js is 7.8 MB with magic header 1B 43 53 49 01 (not real JS). Identify the install host/CI runner and the account. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill any orphaned temp-dir process, downgrade to 8.13.0, purge npm cache, and rotate every credential/browser session and crypto-wallet seed on that machine. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet and all CI runners for the intro.js path and payload hashes, and pivot to the execution/C2 UCs to find the detached stealer and its egress.

| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where (FileName =~ "intro.js" and FolderPath has @"\jscrambler\dist\")

     or SHA256 in ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd","b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903","c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent

| where (TargetFileName =~ "intro.js" and (TargetFilePath has @"\jscrambler\dist\" or TargetFilePath has "/jscrambler/dist/"))

Detached temp-dir dotfile stealer launched by npm/node preinstall hook AIInstallation High
Hunts the execution stage: the jscrambler preinstall loader (dist/setup.js) decompressing the platform payload to a randomly named dotfile in the OS temp dir and spawning it detached from the npm install tree. Article-specific via the node/npm parent, the temp-dir dotfile pattern, and the three payload hashes. Rationale: Combines the article's process-tree (npm/node parent → randomly named .dotfile in OS temp, .exe on Windows) with the three extracted payload hashes. The parent+temp-dir-dotfile pairing is high-fidelity: legitimate npm postinstall builds do not spawn hidden randomly named binaries detached from the install tree. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/28/typosquatted-npm-packages-used-steal-cloud-ci-cd-secrets/
ATT&CKT1546.016 T1059.007 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Native node addon build tools (node-gyp) writing compiled binaries into temp during install — but those are not hidden dotfiles nor detached
  • electron-builder / pkg / nexe bundling a self-contained binary to a temp staging dir
  • Test frameworks spawning helper binaries from os.tmpdir() during CI
  • Antivirus emulation copying a sample into temp for detonation
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "node-gyp" and FileName !endswith ".node"
Response runbook
1) Triage: on the alerting host, confirm the parent chain is npm/node install of jscrambler and capture the temp-dir binary's SHA256 and command line before it self-deletes. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate the orphaned temp-dir process tree, and block the payload hashes at EDR. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same hash and temp-dir process across the estate, then chase its browser-credential file access and outbound C2 (see the credential-access and C2 UCs).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where SHA256 in ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd","b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903","c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
   or (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","node")
       and FileName startswith "."
       and (FolderPath has @"\AppData\Local\Temp\" or FolderPath startswith "/tmp/" or FolderPath has "/T/"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where SHA256 in ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd","b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903","c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
   or (ParentProcessName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","node")
       and (TargetProcessName has @"\AppData\Local\Temp\." or TargetProcessName startswith "/tmp/." or TargetProcessName has "/T/."))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, SHA256, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

  condition: (selection_parent and selection_child) or selection_hash
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 ((@ParentImage:(*\\node.exe OR *\\npm.exe) AND @Image:(*\\Temp\\.*.exe OR *\\Temp\\.*.EXE)) OR @Hashes:*b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| (SHA256HashData=/^(b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903|fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd|c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd)$/i OR (ParentBaseFileName=/^(node|npm)(\.exe)?$/i AND (regex("[\\\\][Tt]emp[\\\\]\\.[a-z0-9]{6,}\\.exe$", field=ImageFileName) OR regex("/(tmp|T)/\\.[a-z0-9]{6,}$", field=ImageFileName))))
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, SHA256HashData, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

Temp-dir stealer reading Chrome/Firefox credential stores and MetaMask wallet vault AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the credential-access/collection stage: the dropped temp-dir binary opening browser credential databases (Login Data, Cookies, Web Data, key4.db) and Chromium LevelDB extension-wallet stores. Article-specific via the payload hashes as the initiating process plus the exact browser artifact filenames the stealer targets. Rationale: Pairs the exact browser credential-store filenames named in the article (Login Data, Cookies, Web Data, key4.db) and the MetaMask extension ID (nkbihfbeogaeaoehlefnkodbefgpgknn LevelDB) with an initiating process that is either one of the payload hashes or a hidden temp-dir binary — a legitimate browser never runs from a temp dotfile. Cross-checked against: • https://jfrog.com/blog/malicious-npm-packages-chrome-browser-information-stealer/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1539 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate browser sync/backup utilities copying profile databases (run from Program Files, not temp)
  • Password-manager import tools reading Login Data during a one-time migration
  • Endpoint backup agents snapshotting user profiles
  • Security/DFIR collection tools (e.g. KAPE, velociraptor) harvesting browser artifacts during IR
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Program Files\" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("kape.exe","velociraptor.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify the accessing process is the temp-dir stealer (hash match) and enumerate which profiles/wallet stores it touched. 2) Contain: isolate the host, force-terminate the process, and treat all browser-saved passwords, session cookies, and crypto-wallet seeds as compromised — trigger org-wide session revocation for the affected user and freeze/monitor associated wallets. 3) Hunt: correlate with the C2 UC to confirm exfiltration and search other hosts where the same jscrambler version was installed.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","Web Data","key4.db","logins.json")
     or FolderPath has @"\Local Extension Settings\nkbihfbeogaeaoehlefnkodbefgpgknn"
| where InitiatingProcessSHA256 in ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd","b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903","c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
     or (InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "." and (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\AppData\Local\Temp\" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "/tmp/" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "/T/"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","Web Data","key4.db","logins.json")
     or TargetFilePath has @"\Local Extension Settings\nkbihfbeogaeaoehlefnkodbefgpgknn"
| where (ActingProcessName startswith "." or ActingProcessName has @"\Temp\." or ActingProcessName has "/tmp/." or ActingProcessName has "/T/.")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

jscrambler stealer C2 egress to hardcoded IPs and Tor endpoints AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the C2 stage: the dropped temp-dir binary beaconing to the two hardcoded IPs (37.27.122.124, 57.128.246.79) and to check/archive.torproject.org for Tor-anonymized exfiltration. Article-specific via the exact IOC IPs and Tor domains tied to a temp-dir process origin. Rationale: Uses the two hardcoded C2 IPs and the check/archive.torproject.org Tor endpoints captured by Harden-Runner, projecting the initiating process so an analyst can immediately confirm a temp-dir binary origin. IPs had no independent second source at publish time, so the detection also surfaces the initiating process for validation rather than blocking on IP reputation alone. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/stealer-backdoor-found-in-3-node-ipc.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090.003 T1573
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Tor Browser users on the host resolving check.torproject.org (the canonical 'are you using Tor' check)
  • Privacy tooling or researchers connecting to torproject.org infrastructure
  • Shared-hosting IP reuse: 37.27.122.124 / 57.128.246.79 (Hetzner/OVH ranges) later reassigned to a benign service
  • Threat-intel enrichment appliances actively probing the IOC IPs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("tor.exe","firefox.exe","tor-browser.exe") and (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Temp\" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "/tmp/" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "/T/")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the connecting process is the temp-dir stealer (folder path / hash) rather than a real Tor Browser, and capture bytes-out volume. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the two IPs and torproject.org egress for non-Tor-Browser processes at the proxy/firewall, and kill the process. 3) Hunt: pivot on the initiating hash across the fleet, confirm which credential stores were read (credential-access UC), and scope every CI runner/dev host that installed jscrambler@8.14.0.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("37.27.122.124","57.128.246.79")
     or RemoteUrl in~ ("check.torproject.org","archive.torproject.org")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("37.27.122.124","57.128.246.79") or DstHostname in~ ("check.torproject.org","archive.torproject.org")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

        where DNS.query IN ("")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web

     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append

PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:

            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or SHA1 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or MD5 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or SHA1 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or MD5 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

            - 'SHA256=__HASH_PLACEHOLDER_REPLACE_ME__'
    condition: selection

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound Zimbra email from Zimbra-XSS campaign sender 193.29.58.37 with .ICS attachment
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Zimbra Classic Web Client XSS exfil beacon to ffrk.net (CVE-2025-27915 campaign) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Zimbra Classic Web Client XSS exfil beacon to ffrk.net (CVE-2025-27915 campaign) AICommand & Control High
Hunts the in-session JavaScript exfiltration channel used by the Zimbra Classic Web Client stored-XSS campaign: a victim's browser POSTs stolen mailbox/session data to https://ffrk.net/apache2_config_default_51_2_1 immediately after rendering a crafted email. Article-specific because it keys on the corroborated exfil host/path rather than generic beaconing. Rationale: Uses the corroborated exfil host/path (ffrk.net/apache2_config_default_51_2_1) from the CVE-2025-27915 Brazilian-military campaign the article cites; requiring a browser process as initiator ties it to the in-session XSS execution and keeps FPs low. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2025/10/zimbra-zero-day-exploited-to-target.html • https://strikeready.com/blog/0day-ics-attack-in-the-wild/ • https://securityaffairs.com/183085/hacking/u-s-cisa-adds-synacor-zimbra-collaboration-suite-zcs-flaw-to-its-known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog.html
ATT&CKT1567 T1041 T1059.007
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Users legitimately browsing the ffrk.net gaming domain (Final Fantasy Record Keeper) from a personal tab
  • Security researcher or sandbox detonating the sample in the monitored environment
  • Threat-intel enrichment tools pre-fetching the IOC URL
  • Web-content-filtering appliance test-fetching the domain for categorization
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--headless","sandbox") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating browser process and the authenticated user; pull the full URL and any request body size to gauge data volume exfiltrated. 2) Contain: revoke/rotate the affected Zimbra session tokens and password, block ffrk.net at proxy/DNS, and isolate the endpoint if a large POST is seen. 3) Hunt: search all Zimbra users for inbound .ICS emails in the delivery window, check for newly created mail forwarding/filter rules on the mailbox, and pivot on any other host contacting ffrk.net.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "ffrk.net"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","iexplore.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has "ffrk.net" or Url has "apache2_config_default_51_2_1"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstHostname, Url, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpMethod, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Zimbra XSS Campaign Exfil Domain ffrk.net
id: 3f2c8a11-7b64-4d2e-9a0f-1c2e5b8d4a91
description: DNS resolution of ffrk.net, the exfiltration host used by the Zimbra Classic Web Client stored-XSS campaign (CVE-2025-27915).
references:

Inbound Zimbra email from Zimbra-XSS campaign sender 193.29.58.37 with .ICS attachment AIDelivery High
Flags mail arriving from the campaign sender IP 193.29.58.37 (spoofed Libyan Navy Office of Protocol) that carries an iCalendar (.ics) attachment — the delivery vector for the Zimbra Classic Web Client stored-XSS payload. Targets perimeter mail-gateway telemetry rather than endpoint, since Zimbra mailflow is not in Microsoft 365. Rationale: 193.29.58.37 is the corroborated sender IP from the CVE-2025-27915 campaign the article cites; scoping to mail-gateway CEF is the realistic telemetry because Zimbra mail never reaches Defender EmailEvents. Defender/Falcon/Datadog left empty as they don't carry Zimbra mailflow. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2025/10/zimbra-zero-day-exploited-to-target.html • https://securityaffairs.com/183014/hacking/zimbra-users-targeted-in-zero-day-exploit-using-icalendar-attachments.html
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1566
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • The IP is re-allocated to a benign sender after the campaign ends
  • A downstream forwarding/relay rewrites SourceIP so the value never appears
  • Threat-intel replay lab re-injecting the sample from the same IP
  • Legitimate iCalendar meeting invites unrelated to the campaign from a coincidentally shared upstream MTA
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify all recipients, pull the raw message and the .ics attachment, and confirm whether the Classic Web Client rendered it (version < 10.1.19). 2) Contain: quarantine/recall the message across all mailboxes, block the sender IP and any lookalike diplomatic-themed senders at the gateway. 3) Hunt: search for outbound connections to ffrk.net from any recipient, review those mailboxes for attacker-created forwarding/filter rules, and confirm Zimbra is patched to 10.1.19.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SourceIP == "193.29.58.37"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, FileName, RequestURL, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Email where All_Email.src="193.29.58.37" by All_Email.src All_Email.src_user All_Email.recipient All_Email.subject All_Email.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Email where All_Email.src="193.29.58.37" by All_Email.src All_Email.src_user All_Email.recipient All_Email.subject All_Email.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent

| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")

| order by files desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] GentleKiller BYOVD — vulnerable/malicious driver load (ThrottleBlood.sys, vgk.sys, eb.sys) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — No Manners Here: The Ruthless Rise of The Gentlemen Ransomware
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] The Gentlemen ransomware scheduled task creation (name matches gentlemen*) · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Windows Event Log clearing via wevtutil (Security/System) — Gentlemen defense evasion · [LLM] Advanced IP Scanner internal reconnaissance — Gentlemen discovery · [LLM] Volume Shadow Copy deletion via vssadmin/wmic — Gentlemen pre-encryption · [LLM] The Gentlemen ransom note / wallpaper drop (README-GENTLEMEN.txt, gentlemen.bmp) · [LLM] The Gentlemen encryptor binary execution by known SHA256 · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
The Gentlemen ransomware scheduled task creation (name matches gentlemen*) AIInstallation High
Hunts creation, execution, or deletion of a Windows scheduled task whose name matches the string 'gentlemen', an execution/persistence artifact explicitly called out in the Unit 42 report on The Gentlemen (Storm-2697) RaaS. This is a named, actor-specific artifact rather than a generic schtasks pattern. Rationale: Anchors on the article's explicit recommendation to create high-severity alerts for scheduled tasks matching 'gentlemen*'; corroborating vendor reporting also documents scheduled-task persistence (e.g. UpdateSystem) for SystemBC, confirming this actor's reliance on schtasks. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/killing-me-gently-inside-gentlemens-edr-killer-framework/ • https://connect.securonix.com/threat-research-intelligence-62/the-gentlemen-raas-and-the-gentlekiller-edr-killer-framework-389
ATT&CKT1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal app or product genuinely containing the substring 'gentlemen' in a task name
  • Security team creating a hunting/decoy task named to mimic the IOC
  • Penetration testers replaying the TTP during an authorized engagement
  • Backup or config-management tooling that templates task names from a hostname/user containing that string
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","tiworker.exe") and InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and InitiatingProcess chain — confirm the task action (binary/script it launches) and whether the creator is an interactive admin or an automated context. 2) Contain: isolate the host, disable/delete the scheduled task, and capture the referenced payload for analysis before deletion. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the same task name, for README-GENTLEMEN.txt / gentlemen.bmp, GentleKiller drivers (ThrottleBlood.sys), and vssadmin/wevtutil activity on the same host within the surrounding 24h.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "gentlemen"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/create","/run","/delete","/change")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has "gentlemen"
| where CommandLine has_any ("/create","/run","/delete","/change")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: The Gentlemen Ransomware Scheduled Task Creation
id: 8f3c1e42-7d6a-4b21-9c0e-1a2b3c4d5e61
description: Detects schtasks.exe operations referencing a task named 'gentlemen', an artifact of The Gentlemen (Storm-2697) RaaS.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/the-gentlemen-ransomware/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/11
tags:

  - attack.execution
  - attack.persistence
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
