  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: 'gentlemen'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @Image:(*\\schtasks.exe OR *\\SCHTASKS.EXE) @CommandLine:(*gentlemen* OR *Gentlemen* OR *GENTLEMEN*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\schtasks\.exe$/i | CommandLine=/gentlemen/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=schtasks.exe Processes.process="*gentlemen*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=schtasks.exe Processes.process="*gentlemen*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
GentleKiller BYOVD — vulnerable/malicious driver load (ThrottleBlood.sys, vgk.sys, eb.sys) AIExploitation High
Detects load or drop of the specific vulnerable/malicious kernel drivers used by The Gentlemen's GentleKiller EDR-killer framework (ThrottleBlood.sys / ThrottleStop.sys = CVE-2025-7771, plus vgk.sys and eb.sys) to terminate AV/EDR from ring-0. These driver names are named-IOC specific, not generic BYOVD. Rationale: Driver filenames ThrottleBlood.sys/ThrottleStop.sys, vgk.sys and eb.sys are named by ESET, Securonix and Kaspersky as the exact GentleKiller BYOVD payloads (CVE-2025-7771), making a filename load/drop match extremely high-fidelity and article-specific rather than generic BYOVD hunting. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/av-killer-exploiting-throttlestop-sys/117026/ • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/killing-me-gently-inside-gentlemens-edr-killer-framework/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-7771
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate overclocking use of ThrottleStop by an enthusiast/lab user (rare in enterprise)
  • A gamer legitimately running Riot Vanguard where vgk.sys is a signed anti-cheat driver
  • Security-research/red-team lab replaying CVE-2025-7771 with authorization
  • Malware sandbox or detonation VM that loaded the driver during analysis
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "vgk.sys" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("vgc.exe","vgtray.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process that dropped/loaded the driver (InitiatingProcess, e.g. launcher All.exe) and check for a preceding service install / registry driver key. 2) Contain: isolate host, block the driver hash, and if confirmed treat EDR on the box as compromised — validate agent health and re-image if tampered. 3) Hunt: look for AV/EDR service termination, README-GENTLEMEN.txt, scheduled tasks named gentlemen*, and lateral movement from this host in the same window.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("ThrottleBlood.sys","ThrottleStop.sys","vgk.sys","eb.sys")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName has_any ("ThrottleBlood.sys","ThrottleStop.sys","vgk.sys","eb.sys")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Windows Event Log clearing via wevtutil (Security/System) — Gentlemen defense evasion AIActions on Objectives High
Detects wevtutil.exe clearing the Security or System event logs, an anti-forensics step the Unit 42 report explicitly recommends alerting on for The Gentlemen. Targets the exact utility and log names rather than generic log tampering. Rationale: The article explicitly recommends behavioral alerts for wevtutil clearing Security/System logs; anchoring on wevtutil + the cl/clear-log verb + the two named channels keeps this tight and low-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/the-gentlemen-ransomware/ • https://connect.securonix.com/threat-research-intelligence-62/the-gentlemen-raas-and-the-gentlekiller-edr-killer-framework-389
ATT&CKT1070.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin manually clearing logs during troubleshooting or disk-space cleanup
  • Log-forwarding/SIEM onboarding scripts that clear then re-baseline channels
  • Golden-image build pipelines that wipe logs before sysprep
  • Compliance tooling rotating/archiving event logs
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","tiworker.exe") and AccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which channel(s) were cleared and the initiating account/parent — legitimate clears are almost always interactive admin sessions, not spawned by an unusual parent. 2) Contain: isolate host, preserve any remaining/forwarded logs from the SIEM, snapshot the endpoint. 3) Hunt: because logs are gone locally, pivot to SIEM-forwarded copies for the same host and look for GentleKiller drivers, vssadmin deletion, and gentlemen* tasks around the clear time.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "wevtutil.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cl","clear-log")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Security","System")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\wevtutil.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("cl","clear-log")
| where CommandLine has_any ("Security","System")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Advanced IP Scanner internal reconnaissance — Gentlemen discovery AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects execution of Advanced IP Scanner, the network-mapping tool Unit 42 states The Gentlemen frequently use for internal reconnaissance prior to lateral movement. Matches on the binary name and product metadata. Rationale: Unit 42 names Advanced IP Scanner explicitly as a tool The Gentlemen frequently deploy; matching the binary plus its product metadata catches renamed copies. Tiered hunting because IT teams also legitimately use it. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/the-gentlemen-ransomware/ • https://www.cybersecuritynews.com/gentlemen-ransomware-global-attacks/
ATT&CKT1046
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate IT/network admins inventorying subnets
  • MSP or field-service technician mapping a client LAN
  • Vulnerability-assessment engagement using the same tool
  • Help-desk troubleshooting device connectivity
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files" | where not (AccountName in~ ("svc-netmon") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: check whether the executing account is a sanctioned IT admin and whether the host is a known admin workstation; review parent process (unusual parents like a temp-dir binary are suspicious). 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, isolate host and disable the account pending review. 3) Hunt: pivot to SMB session enumeration, RDP, and lateral movement from this host, and check for GentleKiller/ransom-note artifacts in the same intrusion window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "advanced_ip_scanner.exe"
    or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "Advanced IP Scanner"
    or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "advanced_ip_scanner.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\advanced_ip_scanner.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Volume Shadow Copy deletion via vssadmin/wmic — Gentlemen pre-encryption AIActions on Objectives High
Detects deletion of Volume Shadow Copies through vssadmin or wmic, the inhibit-recovery step Unit 42 recommends behavioral alerting on for The Gentlemen. Fires immediately before mass encryption. Rationale: Article explicitly calls for behavioral alerts on vssadmin and wmic shadow-copy deletion; has_all on the destructive verb+object keeps it low-FP and it is a reliable pre-encryption tripwire for this RaaS. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/the-gentlemen-ransomware/ • https://darkatlas.io/blog/how-a-go-binary-locks-down-enterprise-networks-in-minutes-the-story-behind-gentlemen-ransomware
ATT&CKT1490
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Veeam/other backup software running pre-snapshot shadow cleanup
  • Sysadmin troubleshooting VSS or reclaiming disk space
  • Windows imaging/DISM maintenance operations
  • Legacy backup scripts pruning old restore points
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","vsnapvss.exe","beremote.exe") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process — a backup product parent is likely benign; cmd.exe/powershell.exe or an unknown binary parent is high-risk. 2) Contain: immediately isolate the host and halt any in-progress encryption; preserve remaining backups off-host. 3) Hunt: fleet-wide sweep for the same command within minutes on other hosts (self-propagation), plus README-GENTLEMEN.txt drops and GentleKiller driver loads.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName =~ "vssadmin.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("delete","shadows"))
    or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("shadowcopy","delete"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\vssadmin.exe" and CommandLine has_all ("delete","shadows"))
    or (NewProcessName endswith "\\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has_all ("shadowcopy","delete"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Gentlemen ransom note / wallpaper drop (README-GENTLEMEN.txt, gentlemen.bmp) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects creation of the named ransom note README-GENTLEMEN.txt and the desktop-defacement wallpaper gentlemen.bmp, the terminal impact artifacts of a Gentlemen encryption run. These exact filenames are actor-specific. Rationale: README-GENTLEMEN.txt and gentlemen.bmp are documented by ESET/search corroboration as this family's ransom note and wallpaper; a filename-create match is a near-zero-FP confirmation of encryption impact on the host. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/killing-me-gently-inside-gentlemens-edr-killer-framework/ • https://connect.securonix.com/threat-research-intelligence-62/the-gentlemen-raas-and-the-gentlekiller-edr-killer-framework-389
ATT&CKT1486 T1491.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Analyst/IR team staging a captured ransom note sample for analysis
  • Threat-intel researcher unpacking the payload on a lab host
  • Backup restore of a previously-encrypted victim system replaying the note
  • Security awareness/tabletop exercise dropping mock artifacts
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\Analysis\\" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("7z.exe","explorer.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess that wrote the note (the encryptor) and the folder spread — many directories = active encryption. 2) Contain: isolate immediately, kill the encryptor process, power-preserve for forensics, and protect backups off-host. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the same filenames and the encryptor hash, plus preceding VSS deletion, GentleKiller drivers, and gentlemen* tasks to scope the blast radius.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName =~ "README-GENTLEMEN.txt" or FileName =~ "gentlemen.bmp"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("README-GENTLEMEN.txt","gentlemen.bmp")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Gentlemen encryptor binary execution by known SHA256 AIActions on Objectives Medium
Alerts on execution (or write) of the known Gentlemen encryptor/tooling binaries by SHA256, including the corroborated main ransomware binary 22b38dad… A direct hash match is the highest-confidence confirmation of the payload on an endpoint. Rationale: Hash 22b38dad… is independently corroborated as the main Gentlemen ransomware binary (ESET/Kaspersky); the remaining three are Unit 42-published sample hashes. Hash execution is a definitive, essentially zero-FP presence indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/the-gentlemen-ransomware/ • https://securelist.com/av-killer-exploiting-throttlestop-sys/117026/
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analysis lab intentionally detonating the sample
  • Threat-intel retro-hunt uploading the binary to a scanning host
  • Hash collision (cryptographically implausible for SHA256 — effectively none)
  • IR responder copying the sample for evidence handling
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has "MALWARE-LAB" and DeviceName !has "SANDBOX"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host, executing account, and whether this was a detonation lab vs a production endpoint. 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately, block the hash tenant-wide, and preserve for forensics — assume active encryption. 3) Hunt: retro-hunt the hash across all endpoints and correlate with GentleKiller driver loads, VSS deletion, wevtutil clears, and README-GENTLEMEN.txt to scope the intrusion.

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2024-55591", "CVE-2025-32433", "CVE-2025-33073", "CVE-2025-55182", "CVE-2025-7771", "CVE-2023-27532", "CVE-2024-37085")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId

// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2024-55591", "CVE-2025-32433", "CVE-2025-33073", "CVE-2025-55182", "CVE-2025-7771", "CVE-2023-27532", "CVE-2024-37085")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2", "025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", "5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3", "a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718") or SHA1 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2", "025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", "5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3", "a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718") or MD5 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2", "025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", "5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3", "a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2", "025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", "5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3", "a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718") or SHA1 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2", "025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", "5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3", "a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718") or MD5 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2", "025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", "5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3", "a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2", "025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", "5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3", "a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TSDProxy: Internal proxy auth token forwarded to backend services enables management API escalation

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] TSDProxy management API auth-bypass: forwarded token replayed to 127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] TSDProxy internal auth token leakage / capture via backend header reflection
TSDProxy management API auth-bypass: forwarded token replayed to 127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1 AIExploitation High
Hunts for a non-tsdproxy process (curl/wget/python/scripting runtime) on a tsdproxy host issuing an HTTP request to the localhost management port with an injected x-tsdproxy-auth-token or x-tsdproxy-id header against an /api/v1 endpoint. This is the exact replay step of GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8, where a compromised backend forwards the stolen internal token from localhost with an arbitrary identity to gain full management API control. Rationale: Anchors on three product-unique strings from the article's PoC (`127.0.0.1:8080`, `x-tsdproxy-auth-token`/`x-tsdproxy-id`, `/api/v1`) that co-occur only during the token-replay bypass; excluding the tsdproxy binary removes the sole legitimate emitter of that header. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy/GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8/ • https://github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Maintainer or pentester manually validating GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8 against their own instance with curl
  • Internal red-team / vuln-scan tooling exercising the /api/v1 endpoints with crafted headers
  • A monitoring script authored to poll the management API for proxy health that (incorrectly) hard-codes the auth token in its command line
  • Config-management runbook that curls the management API during deployment verification
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in~ ("root") or ProcessCommandLine has "x-tsdproxy-id"  // keep attacker's arbitrary-identity replays; optionally allowlist known admin bastion DeviceName values
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process (FileName) and account issuing the request; if it is curl/python/wget spawned by a proxied backend container/service rather than an admin's interactive shell, treat as compromise. Capture the HttpMethod — GET = enumeration, POST/PUT/DELETE = active tampering. 2) Contain: rotate the tsdproxy internal auth token (restart/redeploy tsdproxy), and set identityHeaders=false or upgrade to >=1.4.4-0.20260603142855-434819b4421e which stops forwarding HeaderAuthToken; isolate the backend host/container that sourced the request. 3) Hunt: pull all /api/v1 access on that host, review whether proxies were paused/restarted or webhook deliveries triggered (SSRF), and look for the preceding token-capture step (see the /debug/headers hunt).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("127.0.0.1:8080", "localhost:8080")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "x-tsdproxy-auth-token" or ProcessCommandLine has "x-tsdproxy-id"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/api/v1"
| where FileName !~ "tsdproxy" and InitiatingProcessFileName !~ "tsdproxy"
| extend HttpMethod = extract(@'(?i)-X\s+([A-Za-z]+)', 1, ProcessCommandLine)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, HttpMethod, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("127.0.0.1:8080", "localhost:8080")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "x-tsdproxy-auth-token" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "x-tsdproxy-id"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "/api/v1"
| where ActingProcessName !~ "tsdproxy"
| extend HttpMethod = extract(@'(?i)-X\s+([A-Za-z]+)', 1, ActingProcessCommandLine)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, HttpMethod, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: TSDProxy Management API Token Replay via Injected Identity Headers
id: 5b1e2f3a-9c44-4a7e-bd21-3f8e2a6c9d10
status: experimental
description: Detects a process invoking the TSDProxy localhost management API (:8080/api/v1) with an injected x-tsdproxy-auth-token or x-tsdproxy-id header, matching the GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8 auth bypass.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8
  - https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy/GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/11
tags:
  - attack.t1550.001
  - attack.t1068
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_endpoint:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '127.0.0.1:8080'
      - 'localhost:8080'
  selection_header:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'x-tsdproxy-auth-token'
      - 'x-tsdproxy-id'
  selection_api:
    CommandLine|contains: '/api/v1'
  filter_self:
    Image|endswith: '/tsdproxy'
  condition: selection_endpoint and selection_header and selection_api and not filter_self
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.command_line:(*127.0.0.1\:8080* OR *localhost\:8080*) AND @process.command_line:(*x-tsdproxy-auth-token* OR *x-tsdproxy-id*) AND @process.command_line:*/api/v1* AND -@process.executable.path:*/tsdproxy
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| CommandLine=/(127\.0\.0\.1|localhost):8080/i
| CommandLine=/x-tsdproxy-(auth-token|id)/i
| regex("/api/v1", field=CommandLine)
| NOT ImageFileName=/\/tsdproxy$/i
| table([_time, aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*127.0.0.1:8080*" OR Processes.process="*localhost:8080*") AND NOT Processes.process_name="tsdproxy" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| search (process="*x-tsdproxy-auth-token*" OR process="*x-tsdproxy-id*") process="*/api/v1*"
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| table firstTime lastTime dest user process_name parent_process_name process
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*127.0.0.1:8080*" OR Processes.process="*localhost:8080*") AND NOT Processes.process_name="tsdproxy" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| search (process="*x-tsdproxy-auth-token*" OR process="*x-tsdproxy-id*") process="*/api/v1*"
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| table firstTime lastTime dest user process_name parent_process_name process
TSDProxy internal auth token leakage / capture via backend header reflection AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for the product-unique secret header name x-tsdproxy-auth-token appearing where it must never appear — a non-tsdproxy process command line or a backend service/syslog message — indicating the forwarded internal token has leaked into a log or is being harvested (e.g. via the PoC /debug/headers reflection endpoint). Under GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8 any backend that logs or echoes request headers exposes the management secret to an attacker. Rationale: The header name x-tsdproxy-auth-token is unique to this product and is a secret that should only ever exist inside tsdproxy's own request path; its appearance in any other process command line or backend log is a direct indicator of the article's token-leakage/capture step, and the PoC's /debug/headers reflection endpoint is included as the concrete harvesting vector. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy/GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8/ • https://github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy
ATT&CKT1528
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A backend developer intentionally debugging identity-header pass-through and echoing headers to stdout/logs during troubleshooting
  • Verbose/debug logging level on a backend that dumps all inbound request headers (misconfiguration, not attack)
  • The maintainer reproducing the advisory with the documented /debug/headers curl one-liner
  • A security scanner probing for header-reflection endpoints across services
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessName in~ ("tsdproxy") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "log-level=debug")  // drop self-emission and known verbose-debug backends
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine where the token surfaced — a process command line (active harvest, e.g. curl of /debug/headers piped to extract the value) is higher severity than a passive log line; identify the backend/service that exposed or logged it. 2) Contain: rotate the tsdproxy internal token by restarting/redeploying tsdproxy, disable identityHeaders or upgrade to the fixed build (>=1.4.4-0.20260603142855-434819b4421e), and scrub/rotate any log store that captured the token. 3) Hunt: from the same host/account pivot to the management-API replay hunt (127.0.0.1:8080 /api/v1 with x-tsdproxy-id) to confirm whether the harvested token was actually used, and review proxy config/webhook changes.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "x-tsdproxy-auth-token" or ProcessCommandLine has "/debug/headers"
| where FileName !~ "tsdproxy" and InitiatingProcessFileName !~ "tsdproxy"
| extend TokenHarvest = iff(ProcessCommandLine has "x-tsdproxy-auth-token", "token_string_present", "header_reflection_probe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, TokenHarvest, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where SyslogMessage has "x-tsdproxy-auth-token"
| where ProcessName !~ "tsdproxy"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, Facility, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] SiYuan Electron renderer spawns shell/LOLBin (stored-XSS-to-RCE via nodeIntegration)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Out-of-band write to SiYuan attribute-view store (data/storage/av/*.json payload plant)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
SiYuan Electron renderer spawns shell/LOLBin (stored-XSS-to-RCE via nodeIntegration) AIExploitation High
Hunts the RCE stage of CVE-2026-50551/CVE-2026-54158: a stored XSS payload in an attribute-view cell fires in SiYuan's Electron renderer, which runs with nodeIntegration:true and reaches require('child_process') to spawn arbitrary host commands. SiYuan is a note-taking app and should never parent cmd/powershell/wscript, so any such child is high-fidelity RCE. Rationale: Uses the exact article-named parent binary (SiYuan.exe) and the nodeIntegration→child_process RCE chain; a knowledge-management Electron app spawning interpreters is near-zero baseline, making the parent→child pair high-fidelity. Cross-checked GitLab Advisory DB (CVE-2026-54158) and the SiYuan GitHub security advisories confirming the same nodeIntegration:true/contextIsolation:false config across the CVE family. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-54158/ • https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/security/advisories/GHSA-phhp-9rm9-6gr2 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-50551/
ATT&CKT1203 T1059.007 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SiYuan community plugins that legitimately shell out (e.g. export-to-PDF, git-sync, or pandoc integration plugins invoking node/cmd)
  • Developers running SiYuan from source spawning node.exe during build/watch
  • SiYuan auto-updater launching a helper/installer process on version upgrade
  • Security tooling injecting into or wrapping SiYuan.exe and inheriting the parent name
  • conhost.exe host allocation appearing as a benign child on interpreter launch
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "conhost.exe") | where not (FileName =~ "node.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--build","electron","webpack"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full child ProcessCommandLine and grandchild tree on the host; benign plugin activity has recognisable args (pandoc, git, node build), whereas RCE shows encoded PowerShell, downloaders, or discovery commands. Confirm SiYuan version < 3.7.0 (vulnerable). 2) Contain: isolate the endpoint, kill the SiYuan process tree, and quarantine the user's workspace `data/storage/av/*.json` files before they re-sync to other devices. 3) Hunt: enumerate every device sharing that user's SiYuan sync/workspace (this bug fires on every peer that opens the poisoned row), review those hosts for the same SiYuan.exe child-process pattern and any outbound C2 from the spawned child.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "SiYuan.exe"

Out-of-band write to SiYuan attribute-view store (data/storage/av/*.json payload plant) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the persistence/plant stage of CVE-2026-50551: the malicious attribute-view cell is written to data/storage/av/<avID>.json and rides workspace sync to every peer. A process other than SiYuan.exe writing to that exact store path indicates manual/malware staging of the payload or an external sync client propagating a poisoned AV file. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact backing-store path data/storage/av/<avID>.json plus the fact that only SiYuan.exe should author those files; a foreign writer surfaces manual PoC-style plants and malware staging the poisoned AV JSON. Corroborated against the SiYuan GitHub advisory and GitLab Advisory DB confirming the storage path and sync-propagation model. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-54158/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-50551/
ATT&CKT1565.001 T1608.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Third-party sync clients (Dropbox.exe, OneDrive.exe, Syncthing.exe, Resilio) writing the workspace JSON — note these are ALSO the legitimate payload-propagation vector, so triage rather than blanket-exclude
  • Backup/restore software (Veeam, Duplicati, robocopy) copying the workspace into place
  • User manually restoring a workspace snapshot or migrating between machines
  • Antivirus/EDR remediation rewriting the file after a scan
  • Text editors or scripts a power-user runs to bulk-edit their own SiYuan database
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("OneDrive.exe","Dropbox.exe","Syncthing.exe","ResilioSync.exe","robocopy.exe","MsMpEng.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: retrieve the written data/storage/av/*.json and grep the cell content for HTML breakout patterns (</textarea>, "><img, src=x, onerror=, <script); a benign SiYuan AV file contains none. Identify the writing process — if it is a sync client, treat as propagation and pivot to origin. 2) Contain: quarantine the offending JSON, block the SiYuan sync channel for the affected workspace, and prevent peers from opening the block-attribute panel until cleaned. 3) Hunt: on every device sharing that workspace, look for the paired RCE signal (UC: SiYuan.exe spawning cmd/powershell/node) and confirm all endpoints are upgraded to SiYuan >= 3.7.0.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FolderPath has @"\data\storage\av\"
| where FileName endswith ".json"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("SiYuan.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath has @"\data\storage\av\"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".json"
| where ActingProcessName !has "SiYuan.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File Browser hook-auth pre-auth RCE: filebrowser spawns shell/recon commands (CVE-2026-54088) AIExploitation High
Hunts the File Browser server binary (`filebrowser`) spawning a shell or OS discovery/tooling child process. Under CVE-2026-54088 an unauthenticated attacker injects shell metacharacters into the login username/password, which `os.Expand` substitutes unsanitised into the admin's hook-auth command, causing the `filebrowser` process to execute attacker OS commands. A file server should essentially never spawn `id`/`whoami`/`curl`/`wget`, so any such child is high-fidelity. Rationale: Uses the concrete vulnerable binary name `filebrowser` (parent) plus the article's PoC injection primitive (shell metacharacters `;`/`$(`/backtick and `id`/`whoami` running under the hook command). A file-server process spawning recon/OS tooling is near-zero in benign operation. Cross-checked against filebrowser.org auth docs and auth/hook.go on GitHub. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m93h-4hw7-5qcm • https://filebrowser.org/authentication.html • https://github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/blob/master/auth/hook.go
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1033 T1087.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin legitimately configured a hook-auth command that shells out to an external auth backend using curl/wget (e.g. validating against an LDAP/OIDC gateway)
  • Custom container entrypoint or healthcheck wrapper also named 'filebrowser' spawning /bin/sh for readiness probes
  • Ops running the filebrowser CLI (`filebrowser config`, `filebrowser users`) interactively from a shell where the parent/child order is inverted
  • Backup/maintenance scripts invoked by a filebrowser-named systemd unit that call uname/hostname
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash") and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"^\s*test\s" and not (ProcessCommandLine matches regex @";|\|\||&&|\$\(|\x60"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree for the alert — confirm InitiatingProcessFileName=='filebrowser' and inspect the child ProcessCommandLine for injected recon (id/whoami/cat /etc/passwd) or separators; correlate to the host's web/reverse-proxy logs for a POST to /api/login in the same second. 2) Contain: isolate the host, stop the filebrowser container/service, and disable hook authentication (set auth.method back to json/proxy) or patch to filebrowser v2 > 2.63.5. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for follow-on egress/reverse shells (UC2), new files under the served directory (webshell/backdoor), new cron entries or SSH authorized_keys, and any outbound connection from the filebrowser process subtree.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "filebrowser"
| where (FileName in~ ("id","whoami","uname","hostname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","netcat","socat","python","python3","perl","ruby","php"))
    or (FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","ash","zsh","ksh")
        and (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/passwd","/etc/shadow","whoami","uname","/dev/tcp/")
             or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @";|\|\||&&|\$\(|\x60"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "filebrowser" or ParentProcessName has "filebrowser"
| where (TargetProcessName has_any ("/id","/whoami","/uname","/hostname","/curl","/wget","/nc","/ncat","/socat","/python","/perl","/ruby","/php"))
    or (TargetProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/ash","/zsh","/ksh")
        and (TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/passwd","/etc/shadow","whoami","uname","/dev/tcp/")
             or TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @";|\|\||&&|\$\(|\x60"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| (ImageFileName=/\/(id|whoami|uname|hostname|curl|wget|nc|ncat|socat|python[0-9]?|perl|ruby|php)$/i OR (ImageFileName=/\/(sh|bash|dash|ash|zsh|ksh)$/i AND regex("(/etc/passwd|/etc/shadow|whoami|uname|/dev/tcp/|;|\\$\\()", field=CommandLine)))

File Browser hook-auth RCE follow-on: reverse shell / egress tooling under filebrowser (CVE-2026-54088) AICommand & Control High
Hunts the File Browser process subtree spawning a reverse shell or ingress/download tool after successful command injection. Distinct from the discovery UC: this targets the C2 stage where the injected command establishes an interactive shell (`bash -i`, `/dev/tcp/`, `nc -e`, `socat`, `mkfifo`) or pulls a second-stage payload (`curl`/`wget` piped to a shell) from the `filebrowser` process. Rationale: Pairs the concrete vulnerable parent binary `filebrowser` with high-specificity reverse-shell/ingress signatures (`/dev/tcp/`, `bash -i`, `nc -e`, `socat`, `curl|wget` piped to shell) from the RCE class described in the advisory. These command-line strings are near-zero-FP and map the exploit to its C2/second-stage phase. Corroborated via filebrowser.org auth docs and the GHSA advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m93h-4hw7-5qcm • https://filebrowser.org/authentication.html • https://github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/blob/master/auth/hook.go
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1105 T1571
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit hook-auth command that uses curl/wget to POST credentials to an external authentication API
  • filebrowser sidecar/init script that pulls config or TLS certs via curl/wget at startup
  • Admin debugging the container with `docker exec` where the shell's parent resolves to filebrowser
  • Monitoring agent invoking python from within the filebrowser service context for metrics
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("curl","wget") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("https://auth.","/certs/","/token") and ProcessCommandLine !has "/dev/tcp/" and ProcessCommandLine !has "| sh" and ProcessCommandLine !has "|sh")
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the child ProcessCommandLine and resolve the destination host/port (grep for the IP after /dev/tcp/ or the nc/socat/curl target); check DeviceNetworkEvents on the same host for a matching outbound public connection in the same window. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the filebrowser process/container, block the observed C2 IP/domain at the egress firewall, and rotate any credentials/secrets readable by the filebrowser service account. 3) Hunt: search for downloaded second-stage files, persistence (cron, systemd units, authorized_keys), lateral SSH from this host, and repeat the UC1 discovery query to scope earlier recon.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "filebrowser"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","ash","zsh","ksh","nc","ncat","netcat","socat","curl","wget","python","python3","perl")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp/","bash -i","sh -i","mkfifo","socat","import socket","import pty","curl ","wget ")
    or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\bnc(\.traditional)?\b.*\s-[ec]\b"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "filebrowser" or ParentProcessName has "filebrowser"
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/ash","/zsh","/ksh","/nc","/ncat","/socat","/curl","/wget","/python","/perl")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp/","bash -i","sh -i","mkfifo","socat","import socket","import pty","curl ","wget ")
    or TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\bnc(\.traditional)?\b.*\s-[ec]\b"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FileBrowser proxy-auth bypass (CVE-2026-54089): direct inbound to app process bypassing reverse proxy AIDelivery Medium
Hunts direct network connections accepted by the FileBrowser (`filebrowser`) process from public/non-RFC1918 sources. In a correct proxy-auth deployment (auth.method=proxy) ALL traffic is fronted by nginx/Traefik/Caddy on loopback; any direct client reaching the app port can forge the X-Remote-User header for full admin takeover, so a direct inbound connection is the pre-condition for exploitation. Rationale: Anchors on the concrete `filebrowser` binary and the article's stated proxy-auth trust model (all traffic should arrive via loopback/proxy). A public-sourced inbound connection is the necessary pre-condition for the header-forgery bypass; cross-checked against GLAD advisory and FileBrowser Quantum proxy-auth docs. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/v2/CVE-2026-54089/ • https://filebrowserquantum.com/en/docs/configuration/authentication/proxy/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqp3-jq6g-x3qm
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Monitoring/uptime probes (Uptime-Kuma, Prometheus blackbox_exporter) hitting the exposed port from a monitoring host
  • Administrator accessing FileBrowser by IP:port directly for debugging, bypassing the proxy
  • Internal vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys/OpenVAS) connecting to the port
  • Public load-balancer or Kubernetes kubelet liveness/health checks against the container port
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the RemoteIP — is it a known monitoring/LB/scanner asset or an unexpected external client? Check LocalPort matches the FileBrowser publish port and whether the host is meant to be proxy-fronted only. 2) Contain: if the source is untrusted, firewall the FileBrowser port to the reverse-proxy IP only (or rebind the container to 127.0.0.1), and rotate the JWT signing key to invalidate any minted admin tokens. 3) Hunt: pivot to the same SourceIP in web/proxy access logs for POST /api/login followed by /api/settings or /api/users (UC2/UC3), and review the FileBrowser user store for accounts created out-of-band.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "filebrowser"        // the FileBrowser Go binary
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"                          // proxy-auth setups should only see loopback/proxy
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationPort == 8085                            // FileBrowser published port (article PoC -p 8085:80)
| where DeviceAction in~ ("allow","permit","accept","") or isempty(DeviceAction)
| where not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP)) and SourceIP != "127.0.0.1"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count() by SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by LastSeen desc

FileBrowser CVE-2026-54089: forged X-Remote-User / X-Original-User header on /api/login AIExploitation Medium
Hunts HTTP requests to FileBrowser's /api/login endpoint that carry a proxy-auth identity header (X-Remote-User / X-Original-User / Remote-User) sourced from the client rather than injected internally by the trusted proxy. FileBrowser unconditionally trusts this header to mint a JWT for any username (including admin) with no password check, so a client-supplied header on the login path is direct exploitation. Rationale: Uses the article's exact vulnerable endpoint (/api/login) and the trusted header name (X-Remote-User, per proxy.go and FileBrowser Quantum docs) plus the documented aliases. A client-set proxy-auth header on the login path is the literal exploit primitive; header capture at the proxy is the only place this value is visible (not in Defender/FDR endpoint tables). Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/v2/CVE-2026-54089/ • https://filebrowserquantum.com/en/docs/configuration/authentication/proxy/
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • The trusted reverse proxy's own hop legitimately injecting X-Remote-User (if the access log records post-injection headers on the loopback request)
  • Security scanners or authorized pentesters testing specifically for CVE-2026-54089
  • Internal tooling misconfigured to forward the identity header
  • Automated SSO integration test suites exercising the proxy-auth flow
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the request SourceIP is NOT the reverse-proxy address — a client-supplied X-Remote-User from any other IP is exploitation. Note the username value in the header (admin = full takeover). 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the proxy/WAF, rebind FileBrowser to loopback, and rotate the JWT signing key to revoke minted tokens; review the impacted account's actions. 3) Hunt: correlate the same SourceIP to subsequent /api/settings and /api/users calls (UC3), and search the user database for accounts auto-created from unknown usernames.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ProcessName in~ ("nginx","caddy","traefik","apache2","httpd")
| where SyslogMessage has "/api/login"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("X-Remote-User","X-Original-User","Remote-User")   // requires log_format that records the request header
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where NOT (cidrmatch("127.0.0.0/8",src))

FileBrowser CVE-2026-54089: admin-endpoint access immediately after /api/login from same client (privilege jump) AIExploitation Medium
Correlates a FileBrowser /api/login request with admin-only API calls (/api/settings, /api/users, /api/resources with write/delete) from the same source IP within a 2-minute window. The proxy-auth bypass lets an unauthenticated client obtain an admin JWT in one request; a session that logs in and immediately performs admin actions with no legitimate elevation is the post-exploitation signature. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete admin endpoints (/api/settings, /api/users) reachable only by an admin JWT, correlated to the /api/login mint within a tight window. The temporal login->admin-action shape captures the credential-less privilege jump the CVE enables without needing header visibility, so it works on plain access logs. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/v2/CVE-2026-54089/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqp3-jq6g-x3qm
ATT&CKT1548 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate administrator logging in then editing settings/users as part of normal workflow
  • Automation or IaC scripts that authenticate then provision users via the API
  • Backup or inventory tooling enumerating /api/resources shortly after auth
  • The reverse proxy's own health probe hitting /api/settings after a synthetic login
Response runbook
1) Triage: check whether the SourceIP is the reverse proxy (expected) or a direct external client (suspicious). Confirm the login used proxy-auth and identify the username/permission set that performed the admin action. 2) Contain: if the client is untrusted, block the IP, rebind FileBrowser to loopback, rotate the JWT signing key, and audit any settings/user changes made in the window. 3) Hunt: pivot on the SourceIP to UC1 (direct inbound) and UC2 (forged header), and diff the FileBrowser user store and settings against the last known-good backup for unauthorized changes.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let Window = 2m;
let Logins = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where RequestURL has "/api/login"
    | project LoginTime = TimeGenerated, SourceIP, LoginURL = RequestURL;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where RequestURL has_any ("/api/settings","/api/users","/api/resources")
| where RequestMethod in~ ("POST","PUT","DELETE","PATCH")
| join kind=inner Logins on SourceIP
| where TimeGenerated between (LoginTime .. LoginTime + Window)
| project LoginTime, AdminActionTime = TimeGenerated, SourceIP, LoginURL, AdminURL = RequestURL, RequestMethod, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by AdminActionTime desc
WEB

| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*/api/login*" OR Web.url="*/api/settings*" OR Web.url="*/api/users*" OR Web.url="*/api/resources*") by _time, Web.src, Web.url, Web.http_method
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| search url="*/api/login*" AND (url="*/api/settings*" OR url="*/api/users*" OR (url="*/api/resources*" AND (http_method=POST OR http_method=PUT OR http_method=DELETE OR http_method=PATCH)))

| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*/api/login*" OR Web.url="*/api/settings*" OR Web.url="*/api/users*" OR Web.url="*/api/resources*") by _time, Web.src, Web.url, Web.http_method

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] SiYuan kernel listening on 6806 with empty AccessAuthCode (vulnerable exposure) · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Non-browser process modifying Chrome/Edge extension files (CRX/manifest tampering)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Browser process connecting to SiYuan kernel admin API on 127.0.0.1:6806 · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Browser process connecting to SiYuan kernel admin API on 127.0.0.1:6806 AIExploitation Medium
Hunts for a Chrome/Chromium/Edge browser process opening a loopback connection to the SiYuan kernel HTTP server (port 6806). CVE-2026-54069 lets ANY installed extension reach this port and receive RoleAdministrator without a token, so browser-originated traffic to the kernel is the exploitation signal. Rationale: Uses the article's exact kernel endpoint (127.0.0.1:6806) plus the requirement that the caller is a browser rendering a chrome-extension:// origin. Corroborated by the GitLab advisory and SiYuan docs confirming 6806 as the default kernel port. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-54069/ • https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan
ATT&CKT1176 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SiYuan's official web-clipper browser extension legitimately posting captured pages to 127.0.0.1:6806
  • User manually opening the SiYuan Web UI (http://127.0.0.1:6806) in a normal browser tab
  • Developer/power user testing the SiYuan API with browser dev-tools or a REST client extension
  • Browser-based automation or bookmarklet integrations the user deliberately installed
  • EDR loopback telemetry being sparse or absent on some agent versions (false negatives, not positives)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "siyuan" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "clipper"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the extension. Enumerate installed extensions on the host (Chrome ...\User Data\Default\Extensions) and compare the browser PID/command line to known-good; check whether the SiYuan official clipper is installed. 2) Contain: if the extension is unrecognized, remove it, force-close the browser, and set a non-empty AccessAuthCode on SiYuan; upgrade SiYuan to >=3.7.0. 3) Hunt: review SiYuan workspace for injected blocks (img onerror payloads), unexpected /api/system/setConf changes, and outbound connections from the SiYuan renderer to unfamiliar domains indicating stored-XSS beaconing.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort == 6806
| where RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","chromium.exe","opera.exe","vivaldi.exe")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Conns=count() by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by FirstSeen desc
